title.narrative: BEST (Beda and Setara: Different yet Equal): Program for Empowering Youth and Religious Actors to Promote Tolerance and Diversity

description.narrative: In October 2021, Bani Abdurrahman Wahid Foundation (YBAW) began to implement a project entitled BEST (Beda and Setara: Different yet Equal): Program for Empowering Youth and Religious Actors to Promote Tolerance and Diversity, supported by The State of Netherlands. The goal of this project is cultivating an inclusive and tolerant society founded on a strong constitutional paradigm in ensuring freedom of religion and beliefs. Outcomes include: • Improving the capacity of agents of change in organization, community mobilization, and advocacy at the quantitative and qualitative levels. • Strengthening the network of young people and religious leader who are active and capable advocates for equality and diversity. • Strengthening collaboration among interfaith groups in facilitating dialogue and advocacy in disseminating principles of Freedom of Religion and Belief (FoRB). • Mainstreaming of the constitutional paradigm of FoRB in the Indonesian sociopolitical sphere, including through advocacy to decrease discriminatory regulations and to increase the number of regulations supporting FoRB, and to raise public awareness and understanding of FoRB from a constitutional paradigm.

organisation.narrative: YBAW was established in February 2012 in Jakarta with the goal to emulate the values, ideas and struggles of the late President Abdurrahman Wahid (popularly known as Gus Dur). President Wahid was considered as the champion of democracy in Indonesia. He had a world reputation as an advocate for promoting dialogue to solve ethnic and religious conflicts. He believed that a more just world order could only be achieved through dialogues and negotiations and not through confrontation and violence. YBAW was established by family members and close associates of Abdurrahman Wahid after he passed away.

There were 94 out of 112 youth leaders and 84 out of 104 religious leaders who filled out the survey. The questions in the survey were intended to clarify the extent to which the participants' perspective about the relationship between religion and the state, their views on tolerance, and their understanding of human rights principles, as well as respect for local wisdom.

To measure the extent of participants' views regarding the relationship between religion and local traditions, this survey proposed the statement "religion should be based on the traditions of the community where the first religion was born, it should not be based on traditions that grew up in Indonesia", there is a change in the number of young people who are doubtful from nine to two persons. Meanwhile, there are still four religious leaders who have doubts. This means that there was an increasing participant that respect local traditions.

description.narrative:
1. Mapping of Youth and Religious Leader We identified potential young leaders and religious leaders in the program area who will be involved in program activities such as: workshop on managing diversity, campaign and advocacy. This process was carried out through consultations with community leaders from religious-based organizations and local communities. We reached many organizations such as NU, Muhammadiya, KWI, PGI, WALUBI, PHDI JAI, and others, as well as youth organizations such as Ansor, Fatayat, Pemuda Muhammadiyah, to obtain recommended potential leaders. In the range between November – December 2021, this mapping has captured 155 potential youth leaders (91 male, 64 female), and 180 religious’ leaders (97 male, 83 female)
2. Community Assessment We carried out assessment activity for two months (November–December 2021) to gather information related to the issue of tolerance and diversity in six regions, including West Kalimantan, West Java, Central Java, Yogyakarta, East Java, and Sulawesi. The assessment aimed at obtaining a real picture of the socio-political context in the region, and to obtain information about the experiences of communities and community organizers in managing diversity issues, and information about the need for capacity building for youth leaders and religious leaders in networking and advocacy area.
The assessment is carried out by targeting communities in the program area, CSO networks, and local governments. We used several methods, including: [1] community needs survey targeting community activists with interfaith work experience; [2] document studies including the results of surveys, research, or studies related to the issue of tolerance and diversity, news in print and electronic media, and social media; [3] The FGDs involved the community and CSOs.

YBAW has used the preparation phase (October – December 2021) to carry out several activities. The first step is to form a program team, then hold a coordination meeting to build an understanding of the program and its implementation strategy. In this phase, YBAW has also taken the initiative to carry out the activity of youth and religious leaders mapping and community assessment

title.narrative: Workshop for Youth and Religous Leader

description.narrative:
Stage One: Module Development As a guide for facilitators to manage the training, it is necessary to develop a module. The module includes a learning framework that explains the objectives, methods and steps in delivering the training material. With the arrangement of the module, it will be easier for the facilitator to guide the learning process when the training class is running, as well as being able to explore basic information about knowledge and experience in discussions with participants.
Stage Two: Recruitment for Facilitators and Facilitation Workshop The selection of facilitators began with identifying the candidate. Initially, YBAW identified people who had experience in facilitating training on diversity issues whether it was organized by YBAW networks or other institutions. This process had recruited 16 people as potential facilitators as candidates to be selected based on their experience and availability. Finally, this process selected 12 facilitators to guide the training of youth and religious leaders.
Stage Three: Workshop for Youth and Religious Leader After preparing the facilitators, we conducted a three-day workshop that invite youth and religious leaders. Initially, this workshop was designed to be held in each region (6 workshops), but because we needed to reduce the mobility of facilitators to go outside amid the high number of COVID-19, we decided to conduct the activity simultaneously by inviting participants from various regions and creating two classes in one workshop.
During this reporting period we held training workshop four times, such as: • Training for youth leaders at the Hotel Museum Batik Yogyakarta, March 25-27, 2022, with a total of 26 participants (13 male, 13 female) • Religious leader training in Makassar, 17-19 June 2022, attended by 25 participants (14 male, 11 female) • Religious leader training at Bumi Wiyata Hotel on 24-26 June 2022, attended by 79 participants (49 males and 30 females) • Youth leader training at Wisma Makara UI Depok, held on 28-30 June 2022, attended by 87 participants (62 males and 25 females)
Overall, the workshop has trained 104 religious’ leaders (63 male, 41 female) and 112 youth leaders (71 male, 41 female), involving 12 facilitators.

Based on the module, the learning materials in the workshop are delivered into many segments during the three-day workshop process, including: 1. Segment 1: Clarifying assumptions and building perspective. The purpose of this segment is to strengthen the sensitivity of participants to the issue of diversity. Participants carried out various exercises to elaborate their experiences on diversity using the "river of life" tool. Then participants were introduced to theories about how perceptions and perspectives are constructed, including: “ladder of inference” and “map is not the territory” theory. 2. Segment 2: Understand "cognitive bias" and egocentrism (memory, myopia, truthfulness, hypocrisy, oversimplification, blindness). The learning process in this segment aims to eliminate negative stigma against different groups and eliminate egocentrism. Participants learn to increase their level of listening, from level 1 (habits of judgment), level 2: noticing difference (factual), level 3: emotional connections (empathic), to level 4: from the future wanting to emerge (generative). Participants then performed an exercise to identify the negative voices they experienced in their environment, including voice of judgment, voice of cynicism, and voice of fear. 3. Segment 3: "Landscape of diversity in Indonesia". The participants discussed with a resource person about the situation in Indonesia from the perspective of diversity, how the recent trend of intolerance is, and how the community and government have responded. Then participants discuss in groups to create intervention scenarios, what solutions and interventions are needed for the current situation. Whether in the running process there may be a change or a turn in direction, and what are the causal factors that change the condition. Then participants were invited to reflect on the various religious views and attitudes of the community, the role of civil society organizations or groups, and state policies, all of which are variables that shape the landscape of diversity. 4. Segment 4: Understanding trends, structures and mental models of actors in diversity issues. In this segment, the participants do a role play with "social presencing theater", then discuss in groups to analyze cases of intolerance using iceberg analysis and U-process adopted from Otto Scharmer's theory. 5. Segment 5: Constitutional rights related to diversity issues. In this segment, participants discussed with a resource person and group discussion to identify violations of constitutional rights in cases of rejection of places of worship, and what should be done when they face cases of intolerance. In this segment, the participants also had group discussions about the universal values of religions that support diversity, human rights and peace. 6. Segment 7: Rethinking a new mental model, redesigning social structures and systems that support diversity. This segment aims to create alternative narratives, campaigns or initiate activities to advocate diversity 7. Segment 8: Leadership enhancement. This segment is to understand the level of leadership by using the theory of "speed of trust" by Stephen Covey Jr., which is useful for building character and competence, understanding the principles of credibility, consistency, alignment, reputation and contribution.

description.narrative:
To expose information about the BEST program to public, we conducted a launching of program. The activity was held on 23 May 2022 at the Millennium Hotel Jakarta, attended by 83 people (54 men, 29 women) from NGO networks, religious-based organizations, media, and government institutions.
On this occasion, YBAW’s Program Manager Suraji conveyed the information about the BEST program, goals, outcomes, strategies, activities, targets and program areas. Meanwhile, Alissa Wahid, as the coordinator of the Gusdurian Network, was present to convey her views on the update issues about diversity in Indonesia. He warned of the challenges of majoritarianism in society which has become fertile ground for intolerant actions, while many local policies are discriminatory due to the practice of favoritism by regional heads who comply with the demands of their political support groups.
The launch event was also filled with discussions by theme "Strengthening Tolerance, Strengthening Indonesia" hosted by Marzuki Wahid (Head of the Fahmina Islamic Studies Institute) by presenting three resource persons: Khoirul Anam Commissioner of the National Human Rights Commission, Hasanudin Ali (Expert Staff of the Indonesian Ministry of Religion), and Nia Sjarifudin Coordinator of the National Alliance for Unity in Diversity/ ANBTI
With the relationship and support from partners and stakeholders who attended the launching, we followed up by building engagement afterward. This relationship has initiated collaborations, such as the Ministry of Education and Culture which has involved us in formulating strategies for preventing intolerance in schools and universities. With the Ministry of Religion, the YBAW’s network is more intensively involved in the "Religious Moderation" program at the national and regional levels.
The Ministry of Home Affairs has also collaborated with our network in three regions (Cirebon West Java, Makassar Sulawesi, and Kebumen Central Java) for the "Indonesia Rumah Bersama" campaign throughout June 2022. We have also communicated with the Ministry of Law and Human Rights to initiate the preparation of city/district guidelines which integrate human rights principles into local policies.
In addition, our collaboration with a network of interfaith youth organizations such as the Indonesian Catholic Church Youth Commission (KWI), Youth Bureau of the Indonesian Church Association (PGI) and the National Alliance for Unity in Diversity (ANBTI) and the Hindu Dharma Youth Association (Peradah) have prepared meeting activities for interfaith youth called “Temu Kebangsaan”. This activity has been supported by the Coordinating Ministry for Human Development and Culture with the target of youth in the Jakarta, Bogor Depok, and Depok areas. Tangerang, and will be conducted in June 2022.
